author: Tobin Smith
title: Clyde residents weigh in on economic development project - NewsBreak
text:
By Tobin Smith ,
1 hours ago
CLYDE, Texas ( KTAB/KRBC ) – As the City of Clyde moves forward with the “Star Clyde” economic development project, officials are hearing citizen feedback on areas of focus and safety surrounding the project.
Change in a small town is almost always accompanied by speculation, but this change has Clyde citizens thinking positively. At a recent Clyde City Council meeting, the city approved multiple zoning changes for an economic development project the city is calling “Star Clyde.”
Clyde’s new development to boost town & local businesses This new project would be similar to the Allen Ridge development near Abilene Christian University. It’s planned to feature new restaurants, retail spaces, a hotel and residential housing on a plot of land near the Hanner Sports Complex and along an Interstate-20 frontage road.
At the Clyde City Council meeting, many residents expressed their support for the new development project. Several citizens brought their own input to the council, as well as what they had spoken about with other members of the general public.
Aaron Young was one of the Clyde citizens who expressed his support, but he also outlined subjects of consideration for the council while the project is still in its planning phase. His first consideration was potential congestion issues along the I-20 frontage road and a lack of access to the project location via the interstate.
“I have raised concerns about the main access point for Star Clyde and was told they will use the new road created for access to the Hanner Sports Complex. I understand that the two-mile frontage road includes one stop sign and three swells before travelers could reach the development, which illustrates the potential for congestion,” said Young.
An Inside Look: Abilene data center opens doors for facility tour The second bit of feedback Young offered was concerning the type of zoning this area would see and its proximity to Clyde schools.
“If it is zoned for anything other than residential, I would respectfully ask whether it is truly ideal to rezone any area adjacent to a school as non-residential,” said Young.
Finally, Young highlighted proper access roads along the southern regions of the project site, and considerations regarding railroad crossings after a recent tragedy that befell Clyde after a fatal train collision took the lives of two young residents.
“I raise this not to assign blame, but to emphasize the safety impacts near transportation corridors are real and deserve careful consideration before approvals are granted,” said Young.
The Clyde City Council is taking in the citizen input, and Clyde City Councilman Bo Davidson added that after seeing more than 50% growth in Abilene’s sales tax revenue due to the AI data center project, they need to capitalize on growth where they can.
“Traffic is increasing a lot, especially down the interstate. This provides an opportunity for us to bring more development to the city, and to get some of that revenue that’s otherwise just passing us by,” said Davidson.
Abilene’s Data Center advances swiftly with 5,000+ workers City leadership for Clyde says they are in communication with both TxDOT and the Railroad Commission to address the points brought up by citizen feedback, and add that there is no official construction start date due to the considerations for the project’s planning phase to ensure citizen satisfaction.
